title: AI Evaluation
subtitle: Knowing whether it actually works, and keeping knowing that

slides.title: LLM eval inherits Module 01, then breaks it
bullets: Classical eval: fixed label set, check equality, done
LLM output is open-ended text -- equality checks stop working fast
The grader is often itself a model, with its own failure modes
Benchmarks decay: fame leaks them into the next model's training data
Same discipline (Module 01), three new structural problems
slides.notes: Set up the whole module in one slide: this is Module 01's evaluation chapter, plus three genuinely new problems.

slides.title: Problem 1: the output space is unbounded
bullets: A classifier emits one of k labels. exact_match works
An LLM emits any token sequence -- many are correct, differently phrased
So you reach for a GRADER: text mapped to a score
The grader's reliability becomes half of your evaluation problem
This is why 'LLM-as-judge' exists, and why it needs its own rigor
slides.notes: Motivate graders as a necessity, not a shortcut.

slides.title: Problem 2: the eval is itself a model
bullets: Judge an LLM with an LLM: you import its failure modes into your ruler
Position bias, verbosity bias, leniency drift, self-preference
A biased ruler biased in the SAME direction as the system is worst-case
It doesn't look like noise. It looks like false confidence
Treat judge reliability as an engineering problem, not a footnote
slides.notes: This is the core thesis of the judge_bias_and_calibration.py script coming up.

slides.title: Problem 3: benchmarks have an expiration date
bullets: A benchmark is only informative if the model hasn't seen the answers
Popular benchmarks leak into pretraining data via blogs, mirrors, aggregators
Contamination: score stops measuring capability, starts measuring memorization
You can't control this by controlling your pipeline -- it's the vendor's data
Response: build your OWN eval set from your OWN production failures
slides.notes: Contamination is the LLM-era analogue of leakage, but you don't own the pipeline this time.

slides.title: Benchmark literacy: know the fine print
rows: Small enough to memorize; toy-function synthesis only
Only ~450 questions; a few items move the score a lot
Preference is not correctness; voter population skew
slides.notes: Every benchmark is a proxy. Every proxy gets gamed once it becomes a target. Read the limitations section before quoting the number.

slides.title: Start from real failures, not a conference room
bullets: Most common mistake: design the suite before you have any users
That suite tests what the team IMAGINES goes wrong -- almost never what does
Correct order: ship rough -> harvest real failures -> build the taxonomy
Turn each distinct FAILURE CAUSE into a rule or rubric criterion
Synthetic/adversarial cases supplement coverage; they don't replace this
slides.notes: Same habit as Module 01's 'read your worst 100 predictions', renamed 'failure taxonomy'.

slides.title: The eval pyramid
bullets: Deterministic: exact match, schema valid, code executes and passes tests -- nearly free
LLM-as-judge: subjective quality, no fixed reference -- expensive, needs calibration
Human: ground truth, calibration, high-stakes calls -- very expensive
Climb the pyramid only when the layer below can't answer the question
Routing 'is this valid JSON' through a judge wastes a month debugging it
slides.notes: Draw it as a literal pyramid. Reach for the cheapest layer that actually answers the question.

slides.title: Golden dataset sizing is a power question, not a vibe
rows: Detect anything short of catastrophic regression
slides.notes: Compute it, don't guess it -- exactly what the stats script demonstrates next.

slides.title: An eval score is a sample statistic, not a fact
bullets: 50 examples at 72% is a POINT ESTIMATE with real sampling noise
Wilson score interval beats the naive Wald interval at small n and extreme p_hat
McNemar's test: the correct PAIRED test for two prompts, one eval set
Paired bootstrap: same idea for continuous rubric/judge scores
All four formulas checked against hand-solved reference values in code
slides.notes: Run the script live here if possible. Point at the self-check asserts as proof of correctness.

slides.title: 72% vs 74%: same true gap, opposite verdict
slides.notes: Identical underlying accuracies both rows. The only thing that changed is n. This is the numerically undeniable point of the whole section.

slides.title: p-hacking your own eval set
slides.quote: Re-run 40 IDENTICAL-quality prompt variants against one fixed 50-example set and some will look like wins purely from noise.
bullets: Same overfitting pathology as tuning against a small validation set (Module 01)
Fix: a locked test slice touched rarely, a wider eval set, correction for multiple comparisons
Distrust any p-value that came from a search over many candidates
slides.notes: This is exactly what iterating a prompt against one fixed small eval set until the number goes up amounts to.

slides.title: The rubric is the product
bullets: BAD: 'Rate helpfulness 1 to 10' -- a number with no construct validity
GOOD: named, checkable, BINARY criteria (grounded / complete / concise / safe)
Neither models nor humans reliably distinguish a 6 from a 7
Ask for reasoning BEFORE the score -- improves judgments, gives you something to read
A rubric change is a prompt change: version it, review it, re-calibrate after it
slides.notes: This is the single highest-leverage design decision in the whole judge-building process.

slides.title: The bias catalog
rows: Judge rates its own model family higher
slides.notes: Every one of these shows up in the first real calibration run most teams do. Budget time for it.

slides.title: The headline result: binary rubric beats 1-10 Likert
bullets: Same simulated answers, same judge biases, scored two ways
Binary rubric (AND of 4 criteria): Cohen's kappa ~0.5 -- MODERATE agreement
Holistic 1-10 score, exact-match kappa ~0.08-0.09 -- SLIGHT agreement
Quadratic-weighted kappa flatters Likert (~0.7) but answers a different question
CI gates should use the unweighted, decision-relevant number
slides.notes: State the actual kappa numbers from the script output. This is the quantitative core of the module.

slides.title: Calibrating a judge against humans
bullets: 1. Score 50-100 real examples with a human, using YOUR exact rubric
2. Run the judge on the same examples at temperature 0
3. Compute Cohen's kappa (self-checked formula, not a library black box)
4. Below ~0.6-0.7: fix the RUBRIC PROMPT first, not the model
5. Re-check quarterly and after every judge-model upgrade
slides.notes: An uncalibrated judge is a random number generator with good manners. Write the kappa number down somewhere permanent.

slides.title: Online evaluation: the production half
bullets: Offline needs references. Production has none -- reference-free judges on live traffic
Filter: which runs get judged. Sample: what fraction. Cap: an actual weekly spend limit
Guardrail metrics (PII, policy) alert immediately; quality metrics are a trend, not a pager
A/B testing an LLM change is still A/B testing -- same paired-comparison discipline applies
slides.notes: Cross-reference the LangSmith track for the concrete tool-level implementation of this.

slides.title: Human evaluation, spent deliberately
bullets: Structured rubric beats freeform 'any thoughts?' -- freeform doesn't aggregate
Measure INTER-ANNOTATOR agreement, not just the average score
Two humans disagreeing as much as the judge means the rubric is ambiguous
Spend scarce human attention on disagreement and uncertainty, not on re-checking easy wins
slides.notes: Human eval is the most expensive tier and the one everything else calibrates against.

slides.title: Eval-driven development: the capstone workflow
bullets: Production failure -> add to golden dataset, tagged by failure taxonomy
Fix -> re-run full pyramid -> paired test against a PINNED baseline
CI gate: absolute floor AND regression delta, both required
The dataset only grows and is versioned -- a ratchet, not a report
Evals are a living asset with a named owner, or they decay too
